Lesson1

Requirements engineering: the seven tasks, from inception to management

⏱ 0:00–0:09 · 9 minutes of speech📽 slides 1–12Part A
Goal of the lesson. Define a requirement, a stakeholder and requirements engineering; name the seven tasks of requirements engineering and the work product of each; explain how a team controls change after a baseline; compute requirements volatility.

Identifiers used in this lesson: US-nn = user story number nn (for example US-03, user story 3); FR-nn = functional requirement number nn; UC-nn = use case number nn; CR-nn = change request number nn.

Today's question slides 1–2

Good morning. Last Tuesday you learned how agile teams plan their work, and many of you left with a few user stories for your product. Today your project enters Sprint 1, and the hour answers one precise question: how does a team find out what its users need, write it down so that a test can check it, and model it so that the design can start? By the end of the Studio, your team will hold the first version of Block 5 — a short requirements specification, a use-case model, a domain model, a traceability matrix and a function-point count.

The hour has four parts. Part one: the seven tasks of requirements engineering. Part two: elicitation — how a team learns from people what they need. Part three: requirements that can be tested, and the document that holds them, the SRS (Software Requirements Specification). Part four: two models — use cases and the domain model — and the second size estimate of the course, function points. Each part ends with a four-minute Active Break. Today serves LO1 (Learning Outcome 1), because requirements engineering is one of the processes that the industry standards describe, and it prepares LO2 (Learning Outcome 2): next week's design starts from the models you build today.

What a requirement is slides 4–5

Start with three definitions.

requirement — A statement of a capability that a system must provide, or of a condition that it must meet, so that a stakeholder's need is satisfied. A requirement says what the system must do or be; it does not say how the system will be built.

stakeholder — A person or an organisation that has an interest in the system or is affected by it: the users, the client who pays for it, the people who operate it, the regulators, and third parties who never use the product but feel its effects.

requirements engineering — The set of tasks and techniques by which a team understands what its stakeholders need, records it in a form that can be checked, and manages its changes for the whole life of the product.

Why does a course spend a whole class on it? Because of the cost-of-change curve you drew in Class 1. A mistake in a requirement is cheapest to correct while it is still a sentence. Once that sentence has become a design, code and tests, each of them must change as well. Many software projects that failed were technically sound: they failed because they built the wrong thing, or the right thing without one of its essential parts. The Canadian case of Class 1 shows the second kind. In its 2018 report on the Phoenix pay system, the Auditor General of Canada found that Phoenix executives deferred or removed more than one hundred important pay-processing functions, and that the department did not test Phoenix as a whole system before it went live (Report 1 — Building and Implementing the Phoenix Pay System, paragraphs 1.33 and 1.38↗scan). Requirements that are removed without control, and never checked as a whole, reach the users as missing pay.

The international reference for this work is ISO/IEC/IEEE 29148 (International Organization for Standardization / International Electrotechnical Commission / Institute of Electrical and Electronics Engineers standard 29148), Systems and software engineering — Life cycle processes — Requirements engineering (its page at the International Organization for Standardization↗scan). It defines the requirements-engineering processes, the characteristics of a good requirement and the content of the requirements documents. We use a short subset of it today.

The seven tasks (1/2): inception, elicitation, elaboration slide 6

Your textbook, Pressman and Maxim, 9th edition, chapter 7↗scan, describes requirements engineering as seven tasks. Read them as seven kinds of work, not as seven phases done once and in order: they overlap, and in an iterative process a team performs a little of each in every iteration. Each task produces its own work product.

  1. inception — The team establishes a first, shared understanding of the problem: who asks for a solution, who will use it, what kind of solution is wanted, and how well the people involved communicate. Work product: a vision statement, a first list of stakeholders, a first scope.
  2. elicitation — The team draws the needs out of the stakeholders — by asking, by observing, by showing prototypes — and records them. Work product: interview notes, observations, user stories. Lesson 2 is about this task.
  3. elaboration — The team refines the raw needs into models: scenarios, use cases, classes and their relationships. Work product: the analysis model — Lessons 4 and 5.

The seven tasks (2/2): negotiation, specification, validation, management slide 7

  1. negotiation — The team reconciles requirements that conflict with each other, or with the time and money available: it ranks them by priority, discusses their cost and risk, and reaches an agreement in which each party obtains part of what it wants. Work product: an agreed, prioritised set of requirements.
  2. specification — The team writes the requirements down: as a document, a set of models, a collection of user stories, a prototype, or a combination of these. Work product: in this course, the SRS-Lite (a short Software Requirements Specification) of Block 5 — Lesson 3.
  3. validation — The team checks the written requirements for errors: ambiguity, inconsistency, omissions, statements that no test could check, requirements that nobody asked for; usually in a review with the stakeholders. Work product: a list of defects and their corrections, then an approved version.
  4. management — The team identifies, controls and tracks the requirements and their changes for the whole life of the product. Work product: a baseline, the change requests with their decisions, a traceability matrix.

requirements validation — The task of checking that the written requirements state what the stakeholders actually need — complete, consistent, unambiguous and testable — before they are designed and built. It examines the requirements, not the code; checking the code against the requirements is verification, in Class 7.

None of the seven tasks belongs to one person: the whole team takes part, and so do the stakeholders.

Requirements change — plan for it slide 8

Requirements change. Users understand what they need when they see a first version; the client's priorities move; a law or a campus rule changes. A team cannot stop that; it can control it, with four ideas.

baseline — A reviewed and agreed version of the requirements — for example "version 1.0" — that can be changed only through a defined change-control procedure.

change request — A written proposal to change a baselined requirement: what should change, why, and who asks for it.

impact analysis — The study of everything that a proposed change would affect — other requirements, models, code, tests, the schedule — carried out before anyone decides.

requirements volatility — The rate at which the requirements change during a period: (requirements added + deleted + modified) ÷ (number of requirements in the baseline at the start of the period), usually given as a percentage.

The change-control loop has five steps: a change request is written; an impact analysis lists what the change touches; the team and the stakeholder who decides accept, defer or reject it; an accepted change produces a new version of the baseline; and every link and every test that the change touches is updated. To find what a change touches, the team follows its traceability links — from each requirement back to its source and forward to its models and tests. Lesson 5 builds those links.

A worked number: a baseline holds 10 functional requirements. In two weeks one requirement is added, none is deleted and two are modified. The volatility is (1 + 0 + 2) ÷ 10 = 30 %. A high value is not a failure — it shows that the users are still learning what they need — but it tells the team to keep the change loop running and the links up to date.

Real-life example

HabitHub: one need through the seven tasks, then one change request

Team Wren · HabitHub · fictional
TaskTeam Wren (fictional) builds HabitHub: students track daily habits and streaks, with a weekly report. The team follows one stakeholder need — “remind me before I lose my streak” — through the seven tasks of requirements engineering, then handles change request CR-01 (change request number 1), which arrives after the baseline, and measures the requirements volatility of the first two weeks.
Relation to the lectureIt applies Lesson 1: each task produces its own work product; a change after the baseline goes through change control — request, impact analysis, decision, new version — and volatility measures how much the requirements moved.

Inception. The vision card of Block 1 says: HabitHub helps students keep their daily habits. The stakeholders are the students, a student-wellness coordinator who acts as the client, and the team.

Elicitation. In the interview, one student says: “I forget to check in after 22:00, and I lose my forty-day streak.” The team records the sentence word for word.

Elaboration. The need becomes a scenario — the student picks a reminder time; at that time, if the habit is not checked in, HabitHub shows a reminder — and then use case UC-02 (use case number 2), Set reminder, with a main flow and two alternative flows.

Negotiation. The coordinator wants a reminder every hour, to raise engagement; the students say that more than three reminders a day is annoying. The team proposes, and both sides accept: at most three reminders per habit per day, at times the student chooses. Priority: Must.

Specification. FR-04 (functional requirement number 4): The system shall let a student set up to three reminder times per habit per day, and shall show a reminder at each set time if the habit has not been checked in that day. Verification: set three times, try a fourth — refused; check in before a reminder — no reminder appears.

Validation. The review with the coordinator and two students finds one ambiguity: “per day” in which time zone? The answer — the student's own time zone — is written into FR-04 before the baseline.

Management. The reviewed set of ten functional requirements becomes baseline version 1.0, tagged block5-draft on October 25. On November 2 the coordinator sends CR-01: weekend-only reminders. The impact analysis follows the traceability links of FR-04 and FR-07 (the weekly report): two requirements, two stories, two use cases and three tests to revisit — nine artefacts. The team accepts the change as a Should; the baseline becomes version 1.1, with one new requirement, FR-11.

Volatility. In the first two weeks after the baseline: one requirement added, none deleted, two modified. (1 + 0 + 2) ÷ 10 = 30 %. The team concludes that elicitation is not finished, and plans a second, shorter interview before the Mid-Term.

HabitHub — one need through the seven tasks, then change request CR-01

TaskWalk one HabitHub need through the seven tasks — each task prints its work product and updates the status of the requirement record — then process change request CR-01: list every artefact linked to the requirements it modifies (impact analysis), record the decision and the new baseline version, and compute the requirements volatility.

The program runs here step by step from a recording of its real execution (nothing runs in your browser). To run it yourself, use any Python 3.8 or newer on your own computer: python3 demo1_habithub_requirements_pipeline.py (Legal Notice, section 10↗: your own equipment, your own responsibility; Annex C↗: check every download). Every line of code has a comment line above it.

demo1_habithub_requirements_pipeline.pyready
# =============================================================================# CS 330 - Software Engineering · Class 5 · Lesson 1 · Demo 1# HabitHub: one need through the seven tasks of requirements engineering,# then one change request after the baseline.## TASK: follow one stakeholder need of the fictional product HabitHub (Team#   Wren) through inception, elicitation, elaboration, negotiation,#   specification, validation and management; then handle change request#   CR-01, which arrives after the baseline: list the artefacts it touches#   (impact analysis over the traceability links), record the decision and#   the new baseline version, and compute the requirements volatility of the#   first two weeks.# RELATION TO THE LECTURE: Lesson 1 - every task of requirements engineering#   produces its own work product; after the baseline, a change goes through#   change control (request -> impact analysis -> decision -> new version);#   requirements volatility measures how much the requirements changed.## Educational material - Cyber.SoHo Educational Hub, (c) 2026. Fictional data# only. Licensed for personal study; use is governed by the Cyber.SoHo Legal# Notice, Terms of Use and Acceptable Use Policy:# https://cyber-soho.github.io/prevmon/00.01.%20cyber.soho%20-%20legal.html# Run it with any Python 3.8 or newer, on your own computer:#   python3 demo1_habithub_requirements_pipeline.py# ============================================================================= # TASKS holds the seven tasks of requirements engineering in Pressman's order;# a list keeps that order, so the loop further down visits the tasks one by one.TASKS = ["inception", "elicitation", "elaboration", "negotiation",         # The list continues on this line with the last three of the seven tasks.         "specification", "validation", "management"] # OUTPUTS maps each task to the work product Team Wren obtained in it for one# need; a dictionary lets the loop look the product up by the task's name.OUTPUTS = {    # Inception: a first, shared idea of the problem and of who wants it solved.    "inception": "vision card - HabitHub helps students keep their daily habits",    # Elicitation: the need in the stakeholder's own words, from an interview.    "elicitation": "interview - 'I forget to check in after 22:00 and lose my streak'",    # Elaboration: the need refined into a model - a use case with its flows.    "elaboration": "use case UC-02 Set reminder - a main flow and 2 alternative flows",    # Negotiation: the client wanted hourly reminders, the students wanted few.    "negotiation": "agreed - at most 3 reminders per habit per day, at times the student picks",    # Specification: the agreed need written as one testable 'shall' statement.    "specification": "FR-04 - the system shall let a student set up to 3 reminder times per habit",    # Validation: a review with the stakeholders found one ambiguity and fixed it.    "validation": "review - 1 ambiguity: 'per day' in which time zone? -> the student's own",    # Management: the reviewed set is frozen as version 1.0 and tagged in Git.    "management": "baseline v1.0 - 10 functional requirements, Git tag block5-draft",# The closing brace ends the dictionary of work products.} # The requirement record starts as a bare need; the loop updates its status.requirement = {"id": "FR-04", "status": "need", "version": None} # enumerate() numbers the tasks from 1, so the printout reads 'Task 1 ... Task 7'.for number, task in enumerate(TASKS, start=1):    # Print the number, the task name padded to 13 characters, and its product.    print(f"Task {number} {task:<13}: {OUTPUTS[task]}")    # Record the task just finished as the current status of the requirement.    requirement["status"] = task # After the management task, the requirement belongs to version 1.0 of the baseline.requirement["version"] = "1.0"# Show the record: its identifier, its baseline version and the last task done.print(f"{requirement['id']} is in baseline v{requirement['version']} after '{requirement['status']}'") # TRACE stores the traceability links of three baselined requirements: the# story each comes from, the use case that models it and the tests that check it.TRACE = {    # FR-04 (reminders) comes from US-03, is modelled in UC-02 and has 2 tests.    "FR-04": ["US-03", "UC-02", "test T-04a", "test T-04b"],    # FR-07 (weekly report) comes from US-05, is modelled in UC-04, has 1 test.    "FR-07": ["US-05", "UC-04", "test T-07a"],    # FR-09 (streak counter) is linked too, but the change below does not touch it.    "FR-09": ["US-01", "UC-01", "test T-09a"],# The closing brace ends the dictionary of traceability links.} # CR-01 says what it asks, who asks, and which requirements it modifies, adds, deletes.CHANGE_REQUEST = {"id": "CR-01", "asks": "weekend-only reminders",                  # The person who asks for the change, and the requirements it modifies.                  "requester": "student-wellness coordinator", "modifies": ["FR-04", "FR-07"],                  # One new requirement is needed; none is deleted.                  "adds": ["FR-11"], "deletes": []} # Print the request, so that everyone sees what is asked and by whom.print(f"{CHANGE_REQUEST['id']} from the {CHANGE_REQUEST['requester']}: {CHANGE_REQUEST['asks']}") # impacted collects every artefact linked to a requirement that the change modifies.impacted = []# Visit each modified requirement in turn.for req_id in CHANGE_REQUEST["modifies"]:    # Add the requirement itself: it must be rewritten and reviewed again.    impacted.append(req_id)    # Add every story, use case and test linked to it: each must be checked again.    impacted.extend(TRACE[req_id]) # Print the impact analysis: how many artefacts to revisit, and which ones.print(f"Impact analysis: {len(impacted)} artefacts to revisit -> {', '.join(impacted)}") # The team decides after the analysis; here it accepts the change as a 'Should'.decision = "accepted (priority: Should)"# An accepted change creates a new version of the baseline: 1.0 becomes 1.1.requirement["version"] = "1.1"# Print the decision and the new version: the change-control loop is closed.print(f"Decision: {decision}; the baseline becomes v{requirement['version']}") # The baseline held 10 functional requirements when it was frozen.baseline_size = 10# Count the three kinds of change made by CR-01: added, deleted and modified.changes = len(CHANGE_REQUEST["adds"]) + len(CHANGE_REQUEST["deletes"]) + len(CHANGE_REQUEST["modifies"])# Volatility = changes / size of the baseline, expressed as a percentage.volatility = changes / baseline_size * 100# Print the formula with its numbers, so the result can be checked by hand.print(f"Requirements volatility (first 2 weeks): {changes} / {baseline_size} = {volatility:.0f} %")

#linewhereeventwhat changedprinted
What happens, step by step
  1. The first statement builds the list TASKS with the seven tasks in Pressman's order. A list keeps its order, so every loop over it visits inception first and management last — exactly the order of the pipeline drawn in the visualisation.
  2. The dictionary OUTPUTS links each task name to the work product Team Wren obtained in that task. Watch the step pointer move through its seven entries: Python builds the dictionary line by line before it assigns it to the name OUTPUTS.
  3. requirement is the record that the program updates: an identifier, a status and a version. It starts with the status need and no version.
  4. The for loop uses enumerate(TASKS, start=1) to get both a number and a task name. Each iteration prints one line of the work-product table and then writes the task into requirement["status"]. In the visualisation, one box of the pipeline lights up per iteration.
  5. After the loop the record receives version 1.0: the requirement now belongs to the baseline. The print line confirms it.
  6. TRACE holds the traceability links and CHANGE_REQUEST holds CR-01. The impact-analysis loop visits the two requirements that CR-01 modifies and collects each requirement plus every story, use case and test linked to it — nine artefacts, which light up in the visualisation.
  7. The last block records the decision and the new version 1.1, then computes the volatility: len(adds) + len(deletes) + len(modifies) = 1 + 0 + 2 = 3 changes, divided by the 10 requirements of the baseline, times 100 — 30 %. The gauge in the visualisation fills to that value.

Flash-cards
Five flash-cards for Lesson 1
Read the front, say the definition aloud, then click the card to check yourself.
requirementclick to flip
A statement of a capability that a system must provide, or a condition it must meet, so that a stakeholder's need is satisfied. It says what, not how.
requirements engineeringclick to flip
The set of tasks and techniques by which a team understands what its stakeholders need, records it in a form that can be checked, and manages its changes for the whole life of the product.
the seven tasksclick to flip
Inception · elicitation · elaboration · negotiation · specification · validation · management (Pressman and Maxim, chapter 7). They overlap and repeat in every iteration.
baseline and change requestclick to flip
A baseline is a reviewed, agreed version of the requirements that changes only through change control; a change request is the written proposal — what, why, who asks — that starts that procedure.
requirements volatilityclick to flip
(Added + deleted + modified requirements) ÷ requirements in the baseline, for one period, as a percentage. Example: (1 + 0 + 2) ÷ 10 = 30 %.

Lesson2
Elicitation: stakeholders, techniques, questions and the three classic problems
⏱ 0:13–0:22 · 9 minutes of speech📽 slides 13–21Part B
Goal of the lesson. Define elicitation and tacit knowledge; identify the stakeholders and their viewpoints; choose an elicitation technique for a situation; write open, closed and probing questions in the order of a funnel; name the three classic problems of elicitation — scope, understanding, volatility — and a remedy for each.
Identifiers used in this lesson: US-nn = user story number nn (for example US-03, user story 3).
What elicitation is slides 13–14


elicitation — The task of requirements engineering in which the team draws the needs out of the stakeholders — by asking, observing and showing — and records what it learns, in the stakeholders' own words, before anyone writes a requirement.




Why “draw out” and not simply “collect”? Because the requirements are not written down anywhere, ready to be collected. People know their work very well, but they describe it incompletely. The most important part of what they know is often the part they never mention.




tacit knowledge — Knowledge that a person uses every day in their work but does not put into words without help, because it seems obvious to them; for example, the cafeteria cashier who always asks about allergies before taking an order.




Your textbook (Pressman and Maxim, chapter 7↗scan) suggests starting with context-free questions — questions that fit any project: who asked for this work, who will use the solution, what benefit a good solution would bring, and whether another source for the solution already exists. Next come questions about the problem itself, and finally questions about the conversation: “Are you the right person to answer these questions? Is there anything I should have asked?”


Elicitation starts from the stakeholder map you drew in Class 2: users, the client, operators, regulators, affected third parties. Each group sees the product from its own viewpoint — a student, a club officer and a campus manager will each describe a different product. Conflicts between viewpoints are normal; they are settled later, in negotiation.
Elicitation techniques (1/2): interview, workshop, observation slide 15
Professional guides describe the same core set of techniques. The BABOK Guide (A Guide to the Business Analysis Body of Knowledge), published by the IIBA (International Institute of Business Analysis) and presented on its official page↗scan, lists interviews, workshops, observation, survey or questionnaire, prototyping, brainstorming, focus groups, document analysis and interface analysis among its techniques. The IREB (International Requirements Engineering Board), which certifies requirements engineers with its CPRE (Certified Professional for Requirements Engineering) scheme (the Foundation Level page↗scan), groups them in its Foundation Level syllabus into questioning, collaboration, observation and artefact-based techniques. Here are the seven you need.




interview — A conversation with one stakeholder, or a small group, guided by prepared questions. Structured interviews follow a fixed list; semi-structured interviews start from a list and follow up on the answers; unstructured interviews start from one topic.


requirements workshop — A facilitated meeting in which several stakeholders define, discuss and agree requirements together. A well-known structured form is JAD (Joint Application Design), developed at IBM (International Business Machines) in the late 1970s and usually credited to Chuck Morris and Tony Crawford.


observation — Watching users do their real work, in their real setting, and recording what they do — including what they would never think to say. It is the main technique for bringing tacit knowledge to light.




Interviews are good for depth and for the reasons behind a need; they cost time per person. Workshops settle conflicts between viewpoints quickly, but they need a facilitator and the right people in the room. Observation reveals what people actually do, which can differ from what they say they do; it is slow, and people may behave differently while they are watched.
Elicitation techniques (2/2): questionnaire, prototype, brainstorming, document analysis slide 16


questionnaire (or survey) — A fixed set of written questions sent to many people at once. It is good for counts, frequencies and priorities across a large group; it is weak for “why”, because nobody can ask a follow-up question.


prototype — A quick, partial model of the product — a paper sketch, a set of screens, a clickable mock-up — shown to users so that they can react to something concrete. Users who cannot describe what they need can often say at once what is wrong with a prototype.


brainstorming — A group session that first produces as many ideas as possible without judging them, and only afterwards evaluates and selects them.


document analysis — The study of existing material: forms, policies, manuals, reports, the screens of an existing system. It shows the data and the rules that the product must respect.




No single technique is enough. A team chooses a combination according to four questions: How many stakeholders are there? Is the knowledge tacit? Does a product, or a manual process, already exist? How much time is available? For a campus product built in one semester, a common combination is two or three interviews, one observation of the real activity, and a paper prototype shown to two users.

Asking questions: open, closed, probing — the funnel slide 17
An interview is only as good as its questions. There are three kinds.




open question — A question that invites a description in the person's own words; it usually starts with what, how, tell me or walk me through. “Walk me through the last time you tried to study with a classmate.”


closed question — A question answered with yes or no, a number, or a choice from a list; it confirms a fact. “How many study sessions did you attend last month?”


probing question — A follow-up that asks for detail, an example or a reason about something the person has just said. “You said finding a room took forever — how long, and where did you look?”




Use them in the order of a funnel: open questions first, to let the person describe their world; probing questions next, on the words that surprised you; closed questions last, to confirm facts and numbers. Five more rules make the answers reliable:


    

  1. Ask about the last real occurrence, not about the future. “Would you use a reminder feature?” produces polite answers; “What happened the last time a session was cancelled?” produces facts.
    2. 

  2. Do not describe your solution. The moment you show your idea, people start reviewing it instead of describing their needs.
    3. 

  3. Avoid leading questions — questions that suggest the answer you hope for, such as “Wouldn't it be great if the app booked the room for you?”
    4. 

  4. Listen more than you talk, and write down the person's exact words, not your interpretation.
    5. 

  5. Note the surprise — the answer you did not expect. It often hides the most valuable requirement.
    6. 

The three classic problems of elicitation slides 18–19
In 1992, Michael Christel and Kyo Kang grouped the problems of elicitation into three categories, in a technical report of the SEI (Software Engineering Institute) at Carnegie Mellon University (Issues in Requirements Elicitation↗scan). They still describe what goes wrong today.


    

  1. problems of scope — The boundary of the system is unclear, or the stakeholders give too little or too much information — for example, technical details that belong to the design. Remedy: a clear vision and an explicit scoping decision — your Block 3 — and a “parked” list for good ideas that lie outside it.
    2. 

  2. problems of understanding — Users do not fully know what they need, cannot express it, omit what seems obvious to them, or use words that the team understands differently; different groups disagree. Remedy: several techniques, not one — observation for tacit knowledge, prototypes for needs that are hard to describe, a glossary for words with two meanings.
    3. 

  3. problems of volatility — The requirements change over time, because people learn and the environment moves. Remedy: short iterations and the change-control loop of Lesson 1.
    4. 



One more rule, from the Legal Notice and from Class 2. Interview notes are data about people: use fictional names in everything you write down (Legal Notice, sections 6.7↗ and 18.2), and never record, photograph or film a classmate without permission (section 17↗).

Real-life example
StudyBuddy: six questions, three answers, one surprise
Team Lynx · StudyBuddy · fictional
TaskTeam Lynx (fictional) prepares six interview questions — two open, two closed, two probing — for its partner team, who play the users of StudyBuddy, an app for finding study partners and booking study sessions. After the interview, the team turns the recorded answers into needs, sorts each need as inside or outside the Block 3 scope, and finds the surprise: the one need inside the scope that no user story covers yet.
Relation to the lectureIt applies Lesson 2: the three kinds of question in the order of a funnel, the stakeholder's own words, the problem of understanding — the surprise is tacit knowledge brought into words — and the problem of scope.
The six questions (two of each kind, asked in the order of a funnel, except the closed ones, which the team kept in the middle to save time):


    

  1. (open) Walk me through the last time you tried to study with a classmate.
    2. 

  2. (open) What do you do when a study session is cancelled at the last minute?
    3. 

  3. (closed) Do you study with people who are not in your own course?
    4. 

  4. (closed) How many study sessions did you attend last month?
    5. 

  5. (probing) You said finding a room took forever — how long, and where did you look?
    6. 

  6. (probing) You mentioned your partner did not show up — what would have helped?
    7. 



Three useful answers, in the users' own words (fictional): “We agreed on chat, then nobody booked a room and we ended up in the cafeteria.” — “About 25 minutes, walking between three floors of the library.” — “A reminder an hour before, and a button to say I cannot come.”


The surprise. After question 3, two of the three “users” said they look for partners who write the same exam on the same day, whatever their course. Team Lynx had built its stories around the course code. The need is inside the Block 3 scope, and no story covers it: it becomes US-07 (user story number 7) — As a student, I want to find partners by exam date, so that we prepare for the same exam.


Sorting the needs. Find a free study room is outside the scope — StudyBuddy does not manage rooms — so it is parked, not lost. A reminder before a session and tell the partner I cannot come are already covered by stories. Find partners by exam date is the surprise.

Demo program
StudyBuddy — classify the questions, find the needs and the surprise
demo2_studybuddy_interview.py
TaskClassify Team Lynx's six interview questions as open, closed or probing from their first words, check the 2-2-2 rule of Lab 05, then scan the recorded answers for words that reveal a need and sort every need as parked (outside the scope), known (already in a story) or surprise (in the scope, in no story).
Relation to the lectureLesson 2: the three kinds of question; the stakeholder's own words; the problems of scope (parked needs) and of understanding (the surprise).
The program runs here step by step from a recording of its real execution (nothing runs in your browser). To run it yourself, use any Python 3.8 or newer on your own computer: python3 demo2_studybuddy_interview.py (Legal Notice, section 10↗: your own equipment, your own responsibility; Annex C↗: check every download). # =============================================================================# CS 330 - Software Engineering · Class 5 · Lesson 2 · Demo 2# StudyBuddy: six interview questions, the needs behind the answers,# and the one surprise.## TASK: classify Team Lynx's six prepared interview questions as open, closed#   or probing from their first words and check the Lab 05 rule (two of each#   kind); then scan the recorded answers for words that reveal a need, sort#   every need into "parked" (outside the Block 3 scope), "known" (already in#   a user story) or "surprise" (inside the scope but in no story yet).# RELATION TO THE LECTURE: Lesson 2 - open, closed and probing questions; the#   stakeholder's own words; the "understanding" problem of elicitation - the#   surprise is a need the users had but the team had not heard before.## Educational material - Cyber.SoHo Educational Hub, (c) 2026. Fictional data# only: the "users" are a partner team, and every answer here is invented.# Use is governed by the Cyber.SoHo Legal Notice, Terms of Use and Acceptable Use Policy:# https://cyber-soho.github.io/prevmon/00.01.%20cyber.soho%20-%20legal.html# Run it with any Python 3.8 or newer, on your own computer:#   python3 demo2_studybuddy_interview.py# ============================================================================= # QUESTIONS holds Team Lynx's six prepared questions, in the order they are asked.QUESTIONS = [    # An open question: it asks for a story in the user's own words.    "Walk me through the last time you tried to study with a classmate.",    # A second open question, about what happens when a plan fails.    "What do you do when a study session is cancelled at the last minute?",    # A closed question: the expected answer is yes or no.    "Do you study with people who are not in your own course?",    # A closed question: the expected answer is a number.    "How many study sessions did you attend last month?",    # A probing question: it follows up on words the user said earlier.    "You said finding a room took forever - how long, and where did you look?",    # A probing question: it asks what lies behind an earlier answer.    "You mentioned your partner did not show up - what would have helped?",# The closing bracket ends the list of questions.] # Closed questions usually start with an auxiliary verb, or ask for a count.CLOSED_STARTS = ("do ", "does ", "did ", "is ", "are ", "can ", "will ", "would ",                 # The tuple continues: two starts that ask for a number.                 "how many ", "how often ")# Probing questions usually point back to something the user has just said.PROBING_STARTS = ("you said", "you mentioned", "what do you mean",                  # The tuple continues: two more ways of asking for detail.                  "can you give an example", "why ")  # classify() returns 'probing', 'closed' or 'open' for one question.def classify(question):    # Work in lower case, so that 'Do' and 'do' are treated the same way.    text = question.lower()    # Test probing first: 'can you give an example' must not be taken as closed.    if text.startswith(PROBING_STARTS):        # The question points back to an earlier answer.        return "probing"    # Then test the starts of closed questions.    if text.startswith(CLOSED_STARTS):        # The question expects yes or no, a number, or a choice.        return "closed"    # Any other question invites a free answer.    return "open"  # counts starts every kind at zero; the loop adds one per question of that kind.counts = {"open": 0, "closed": 0, "probing": 0}# Number the questions from 1 while classifying them.for number, question in enumerate(QUESTIONS, start=1):    # Ask classify() which kind of question this is.    kind = classify(question)    # Add one to the counter of that kind.    counts[kind] += 1    # Print the question number, its kind and its text.    print(f"Q{number} {kind:<7} | {question}") # Lab 05 asks for exactly two questions of each kind; compare the whole dictionary.balanced = counts == {"open": 2, "closed": 2, "probing": 2}# Print the counts and say whether the rule is met.print(f"Counts: {counts} -> 2-2-2 rule {'met' if balanced else 'NOT met'}") # ANSWERS keeps the most useful answers in the users' own words, by question number.ANSWERS = {    # Answer to question 1 (Q1): the session never happened - nobody booked a room.    1: "We agreed on chat, then nobody booked a room and we ended up in the cafeteria.",    # A remark made after question 3 (Q3): partners chosen by exam date, not course.    3: "I look for anyone who writes the same exam on the same day, any course.",    # Answer to question 5 (Q5): the time lost in looking for a free room.    5: "About 25 minutes, walking between three floors of the library.",    # Answer to question 6 (Q6): what would have helped when the partner did not come.    6: "A reminder an hour before, and a button to say I cannot come.",# The closing brace ends the dictionary of answers.} # NEED_WORDS links a word heard in an answer to the need that the word reveals.NEED_WORDS = {"room": "find a free study room", "remind": "reminder before a session",              # The dictionary continues with two more words and their needs.              "cannot come": "tell the partner I cannot come", "exam": "find partners by exam date"}# SCOPE lists the needs that lie inside StudyBuddy's Block 3 scoping decision.SCOPE = {"reminder before a session", "tell the partner I cannot come", "find partners by exam date"}# STORY_NEEDS lists the needs that the team's user stories already cover.STORY_NEEDS = {"reminder before a session", "tell the partner I cannot come"} # needs collects every need found, in the order it is heard, without duplicates.needs = []# Visit the answers in the order of their question numbers.for q_number in sorted(ANSWERS):    # Work on a lower-case copy of the answer, so that matching ignores capitals.    answer = ANSWERS[q_number].lower()    # Test every word of NEED_WORDS against this answer.    for word, need in NEED_WORDS.items():        # Keep the need when its word occurs in the answer and the need is new.        if word in answer and need not in needs:            # Remember the need.            needs.append(need)            # Print where the need was heard and which word revealed it.            print(f"Q{q_number}: '{word}' -> need: {need}") # Sort every need into one of three groups.for need in needs:    # A need outside the scoping decision is parked: not built this semester.    if need not in SCOPE:        # Print the parked need.        print(f"PARKED   {need} (outside the Block 3 scope)")    # A need inside the scope but in no user story is the surprise.    elif need not in STORY_NEEDS:        # Print the surprise and the new user story it becomes.        print(f"SURPRISE {need} -> new user story US-07")    # Every other need is already covered by a user story.    else:        # Print the known need.        print(f"KNOWN    {need} (already in a user story)")
Visualisation of the lecture idea
Variables (yellow = changed by this step)
Program output
Execution steps — every step so far; click a row to go back to it
#linewhereeventwhat changedprinted
What happens, step by step
  1. QUESTIONS holds the six questions in the order the team asks them. CLOSED_STARTS and PROBING_STARTS are tuples of typical first words; a tuple is used because str.startswith() accepts a tuple and tests every entry in one call.
  2. The function classify() puts the question in lower case and tests the probing starts first. The order matters: “can you give an example” begins like a closed question (“can …”), but it is a probing one.
  3. The first loop calls classify() for each question and adds one to the matching counter in counts. In the visualisation, each question card drops into the open, closed or probing column.
  4. balanced compares the whole dictionary with {"open": 2, "closed": 2, "probing": 2} in one expression; the result is True, so the 2-2-2 rule is met.
  5. ANSWERS keeps four answers in the users' own words. NEED_WORDS links a word heard in an answer to the need it reveals — a deliberately simple keyword method; a person still reads every answer.
  6. The nested loops test every word against every answer, in the order of the question numbers (sorted(ANSWERS)). A need is added only once (need not in needs). The visualisation highlights the word found in each answer.
  7. The last loop sorts the needs with if / elif / else: outside SCOPE → parked; inside the scope but not in STORY_NEEDS → the surprise, which becomes US-07; otherwise → known. Pause on the SURPRISE line and compare it with the example text.

Five flash-cards for Lesson 2
Read the front, say the definition aloud, then click the card to check yourself.
elicitationclick to flip
The task in which the team draws the needs out of the stakeholders — by asking, observing and showing — and records them in the stakeholders' own words.
tacit knowledgeclick to flip
Knowledge a person uses every day but does not put into words without help, because it seems obvious; observation and prototypes bring it to light.
open, closed and probing questionsclick to flip
Open: invites a description (what, how, walk me through). Closed: yes/no, a number or a choice. Probing: a follow-up on the person's own words. Funnel order: open → probing → closed.
prototype (as an elicitation technique)click to flip
A quick, partial model of the product — paper sketch or clickable screens — shown to users so they can react to something concrete.
the three classic problemsclick to flip
Scope (unclear boundary, too little or too much detail), understanding (needs unknown, unspoken or understood differently) and volatility (needs change) — Christel and Kang, SEI (Software Engineering Institute), 1992.

Multiple-choice question Q2.1 · “Do you order lunch on campus more than twice a week?” is…
Hint: What kind of answer does it expect?
Multiple-choice question Q2.2 · Which technique best reveals how the cafeteria staff actually work during the noon rush — including steps they would never think to mention?
Hint: Tacit knowledge is what people do but do not say.
Multiple-choice question Q2.3 · Users omit information because it seems obvious to them. In Christel and Kang's three categories, this is a problem of…
Hint: The three categories are scope, understanding and volatility.
Multiple-choice question Q2.4 · In the StudyBuddy example, which need was the surprise?
Hint: It was inside the scope, but no user story covered it.
Multiple-select question Q2.5 · Which of these are probing questions? (2 right answers)
Hint: A probing question builds on the person's own words.
Multiple-select question Q2.6 · Which practices make interview answers more reliable? (3 right answers)
Hint: Facts about the past, the person's own words, and no influence from your solution.
Active break · ✋ Try-it · 0:22–0:26 · 4 minutes · slide 21
A two-minute interview in pairs
  1. Pair up with someone from another team. Partner A interviews partner B for two minutes: “What annoys you most about booking a study room?” Start with the open question, then ask two probing questions on B's own words.
  2. Write down B's exact words and one surprise.
  3. Swap: B interviews A for two minutes. In the last ten seconds, each of you says the surprise aloud to the other.
No photos or recordings of your partner without permission ([Legal Notice, section 17](https://cyber-soho.github.io/prevmon/00.01.%20cyber.soho%20-%20legal.html#17-recording-sharing-and-confidentiality-of-sessions)); invented names in your notes ([6.7](https://cyber-soho.github.io/prevmon/00.01.%20cyber.soho%20-%20legal.html#67-data-and-privacy-in-laboratories)).
What to look for — the answer
There is no single right answer. A good interview has more answer than question on the paper, at least one probing question built on the partner's own words, and one surprise — something you had not thought of before.

⏱ 0:26–0:36 · 10 minutes of speech📽 slides 22–31Part C
Goal of the lesson. Classify a statement as a functional requirement, a non-functional requirement or a constraint; name the nine quality characteristics of the product-quality model (ISO/IEC 25010 (International Organization for Standardization / International Electrotechnical Commission standard 25010)); rewrite a vague requirement into a verifiable one; describe the structure of a Software Requirements Specification and of the SRS-Lite (a short Software Requirements Specification) of Block 5.
Identifiers used in this lesson: US-nn = user story number nn (for example US-03, user story 3); FR-nn = functional requirement number nn; NFR-nn = non-functional requirement number nn; C-nn = constraint number nn; D1–D6 = the six draft requirements of the QueueLess example.
Three kinds of statements slides 22–23
Every line of a requirements specification belongs to one of three kinds.




functional requirement — A requirement that states a behaviour or a service the system must provide: what it does, for whom, with which input, producing which result. Example: The system shall let a student cancel their own order until 10 minutes before the chosen pick-up slot.


non-functional requirement — A requirement that states how well the system must perform, or a property it must have as a whole: performance, security and privacy, usability, reliability, maintainability and others. It is also called a quality requirement. Example: The system shall load the menu page in under 2 seconds on the campus Wi-Fi for a menu of up to 40 items.


constraint — A limit placed on the solution or on the project from outside the team: a platform, a technology, a law, a budget, a deadline, a standard. The team cannot trade it away. Example: The product shall run in a web browser without installation.




A three-question test sorts any statement. Does it describe an action of the system? Then it is a FR (functional requirement). Does it describe how well the system acts, or a measurable property of the whole system? Then it is an NFR (non-functional requirement). Does it limit how, or with what, the team may build the product? Then it is a constraint. Some authors, and the standard itself, treat constraints as one more kind of non-functional requirement; Block 5 keeps them separate, because they are decided by someone outside the team.
Quality characteristics: the product-quality model slide 24
How do you know which non-functional requirements to write? The product-quality model of ISO/IEC 25010 (International Organization for Standardization / International Electrotechnical Commission standard 25010) — 2023 edition (its page↗scan) — lists nine quality characteristics, each divided into subcharacteristics:


    

  1. functional suitability — completeness, correctness and appropriateness of the functions;
    2. 

  2. performance efficiency — time behaviour, resource use, capacity;
    3. 

  3. compatibility — co-existence and interoperability with other products;
    4. 

  4. interaction capability — how well people can learn and use the product, including protection against user errors and inclusivity (called usability in the 2011 edition);
    5. 

  5. reliability — faultlessness, availability, fault tolerance, recoverability;
    6. 

  6. security — confidentiality, integrity, non-repudiation, accountability, authenticity, resistance;
    7. 

  7. maintainability — modularity, reusability, analysability, modifiability, testability;
    8. 

  8. flexibility — adaptability, scalability, installability, replaceability (called portability in 2011);
    9. 

  9. safety — new in 2023: operational constraints, risk identification, fail-safe behaviour, hazard warning.
    10. 



Block 5 asks for exactly five non-functional requirements, one in each of five categories, and each category sits inside this model: performance → performance efficiency; security or privacy → security — start from the two or three harms of your product, as Class 2 taught; usability → interaction capability; reliability → reliability; maintainability → maintainability.


A requirement may also refer to an external standard or a law. The sign-up pages shall meet the level AA success criteria of WCAG (Web Content Accessibility Guidelines) 2.2, published by the W3C (World Wide Web Consortium) as the 2.2 recommendation↗scan, is an accessibility requirement that can be checked criterion by criterion. A product that collects personal information in Québec must respect the private-sector privacy act as amended by Law 25 (Bill 64 at the National Assembly↗scan; the regulator is the Commission d'accès à l'information du Québec↗scan): a constraint that no team can negotiate away.
Requirements that can be tested: six rules slide 25


verifiable requirement — A requirement for which a finite, affordable procedure exists that shows whether the product meets it: a test, an inspection, an analysis or a demonstration.




ISO/IEC/IEEE 29148 (International Organization for Standardization / International Electrotechnical Commission / Institute of Electrical and Electronics Engineers standard 29148), in its 2018 edition↗scan, lists the characteristics of a good individual requirement: necessary, appropriate, unambiguous, complete, singular, feasible, verifiable, correct and conforming. In daily work, six rules produce them.


    

  1. Use “shall” for a binding requirement. In requirements language, shall states an obligation; should states a goal; may states an option.
    2. 

  2. One behaviour per requirement. Two behaviours joined by and or or become two requirements, each with its own identifier.
    3. 

  3. A number, a unit and a condition for every quality — or a named check. Not “fast”, but “under 2 seconds on the campus Wi-Fi for a menu of up to 40 items”.
    4. 

  4. No vague words. Fast, easy, user-friendly, intuitive, secure, simple, efficient, flexible, robust — none of them can be measured until you add a number or a check.
    5. 

  5. What, not how. “A red button in the top-right corner” is a design decision; the requirement is what the user must be able to achieve.
    6. 

  6. An identifier, a source and a verification method on every line. The source says which user story or interview answer the requirement comes from; the verification line says how a test will pass or fail it.
    7. 

From weak to strong: the QueueLess rewrites slide 26
The same two rows appear in your Lab 05 handout. Read the left column, then the right.






Weak
Strong






“The app should be fast and easy.”
NFR-01 (non-functional requirement number 1, performance): The system shall load the menu page in under 2 seconds on the campus Wi-Fi for a menu of up to 40 items. Verify: stopwatch, 10 loads, all under 2 seconds.




“Users can cancel.”
FR-05 (functional requirement number 5): The system shall let a student cancel their own order until 10 minutes before the chosen pick-up slot; after that, the cancel action shall not be offered. Source: US-04 (user story number 4), interview answer 2. Verify: try at −11 minutes and at −9 minutes.






Look at what changed. Should became shall. The vague adjectives became a number, a unit and a condition. “Users” became a named actor with a limit. And every strong line names the test that will check it: in Block 7, on November 3, those verification lines become your first test cases.
Two helpers: sentence patterns and the fit criterion slide 27
Two published aids help you write the strong version directly.


The EARS (Easy Approach to Requirements Syntax), developed by Alistair Mavin and his colleagues at Rolls-Royce and published in 2009 (Alistair Mavin's page↗scan), gives each requirement one of five sentence patterns, each with its own keyword:






Pattern
Template
QueueLess example






ubiquitous
The ⟨system⟩ shall ⟨response⟩.
The system shall show the price of each menu item.




event-driven — When
When ⟨trigger⟩, the ⟨system⟩ shall ⟨response⟩.
When an order is marked ready, the system shall notify the student.




state-driven — While
While ⟨state⟩, the ⟨system⟩ shall ⟨response⟩.
While the kitchen is closed, the system shall refuse new orders.




unwanted behaviour — If … then
If ⟨condition⟩, then the ⟨system⟩ shall ⟨response⟩.
If a payment flag is missing, then the system shall keep the order out of the kitchen list.




optional feature — Where
Where ⟨feature is included⟩, the ⟨system⟩ shall ⟨response⟩.
Where group orders are enabled, the system shall split the total per student.






The Volere requirements template of James and Suzanne Robertson (the template page↗scan) adds the idea of a fit criterion: a measurement attached to each requirement, against which any proposed solution can be tested. Your “how we verify it” column is a fit criterion.
The Software Requirements Specification slides 28–29


SRS (Software Requirements Specification) — The document that states the requirements of a software product completely, consistently and verifiably, for the stakeholders who approve it and for the engineers who design, build and test the product.




For decades the reference was IEEE Std 830 (Institute of Electrical and Electronics Engineers Standard 830)-1998 (the standard's page↗scan), the Recommended Practice for Software Requirements Specifications; it was superseded in 2011 by ISO/IEC/IEEE 29148 (International Organization for Standardization / International Electrotechnical Commission / Institute of Electrical and Electronics Engineers standard 29148), whose current edition dates from 2018. A revision of 29148 is under way: in October 2026 it is at the Draft International Standard ballot (the draft's page↗scan), and the 2018 edition remains the one to cite.


The standard offers an example outline. Simplified, it has five parts: (1) an introduction — purpose, scope, product perspective, product functions, user characteristics, limitations, definitions; (2) references; (3) the specific requirements — external interfaces, functions, usability, performance, logical data, design constraints, standards compliance, other quality attributes; (4) verification — how each requirement will be checked; (5) appendices.


Your Block 5 is an SRS-Lite (a short Software Requirements Specification): the same logic on two pages, in seven sections — the header, scope, harms and stories (introduction); the elicitation log; the FRs (functional requirements), NFRs (non-functional requirements) and constraints with a verification line each (specific requirements and verification); the use-case model; the domain model; the function-point count; and the traceability matrix.

Real-life example
QueueLess: from six drafts to a verifiable set
Team Falcon · QueueLess · fictional
TaskTeam Falcon (fictional) builds QueueLess, a cafeteria pre-order app. It reviews six draft requirements, classifies each one as a functional requirement, a non-functional requirement or a constraint, finds the defects that make some of them impossible to test, and rewrites them in the row format of Block 5: identifier · “The system shall …” · source · how we verify it.
Relation to the lectureIt applies Lesson 3: the three kinds of statements, the quality characteristics, the six rules of a verifiable requirement, and the SRS-Lite (a short Software Requirements Specification) row of Block 5.

The rewrites. D1 becomes two requirements: NFR-01 (performance — under 2 seconds on the campus Wi-Fi for up to 40 items) and NFR-03 (usability — a first-time user completes an order in under 3 minutes without help). D2 becomes FR-05, the cancellation rule with its 10-minute limit. D3 becomes NFR-02, a privacy requirement written as who may see what: the allergy note is shown only to the student and to the kitchen screen, never in the manager's summary. D4 leaves the specification: the button belongs to the design of Class 6. D5 stays as constraint C-01 (constraint number 1); D6 stays as FR-07.


What the checker can and cannot see. A program can find a missing shall, a vague word, a design word and an empty verification column. It cannot judge whether the privacy check of NFR-02 is objective — it has no number — so it raises a warning, and a person decides. The same split appeared in Class 4: a program checks three letters of INVEST, people judge the other three.

# =============================================================================# CS 330 - Software Engineering · Class 5 · Lesson 3 · Demo 3# QueueLess: a small checker for requirements that can be tested.## TASK: run five checks on each of Team Falcon's six draft requirements - a#   binding "shall", no vague words, no design detail, a verification method,#   and (for a non-functional requirement) a number - print a verdict for each#   draft, then run the same checks on the team's rewritten set.# RELATION TO THE LECTURE: Lesson 3 - functional requirements, non-functional#   requirements and constraints; the rules of a verifiable requirement; the#   SRS-Lite row "ID - The system shall ... - source - how we verify it" of#   Block 5. A program can catch the visible defects; a person must still#   judge the warnings - the same split as the INVEST letters of Class 4.## Educational material - Cyber.SoHo Educational Hub, (c) 2026. Fictional data# only. Use is governed by the Cyber.SoHo Legal Notice, Terms of Use and Acceptable Use Policy:# https://cyber-soho.github.io/prevmon/00.01.%20cyber.soho%20-%20legal.html# Run it with any Python 3.8 or newer, on your own computer:#   python3 demo3_queueless_requirement_checker.py# ============================================================================= # VAGUE lists words that a test cannot measure until a number or a check is added.VAGUE = ("fast", "easy", "user-friendly", "intuitive", "secure", "simple",         # The tuple continues with four more words that sound good but measure nothing.         "efficient", "flexible", "quick", "robust")# DESIGN lists words that describe a solution (how) instead of a need (what).DESIGN = ("button", "red", "colour", "color", "dropdown", "click", "top-right")  # check() returns two lists for one requirement: failures and warnings.def check(category, text, verify):    # failures will hold the defects that make the requirement unverifiable.    failures = []    # warnings will hold the points that only a person can judge.    warnings = []    # Split the text into lower-case words, without commas and full stops.    words = text.lower().replace(",", " ").replace(".", " ").split()    # Check 1: a binding requirement uses the verb 'shall'.    if "shall" not in words:        # Without 'shall' the statement is a wish, not an obligation.        failures.append("no 'shall' (not binding)")    # Check 2: collect every vague word that occurs in the text.    vague = [w for w in VAGUE if w in words]    # Any vague word is a failure until it is replaced by a measure.    if vague:        # Name the vague words, so that the author knows what to replace.        failures.append("vague: " + ", ".join(vague))    # Check 3: collect every word that describes a design decision.    design = [w for w in DESIGN if w in words]    # A design word means the statement says how, not what.    if design:        # Name the design words, so the statement can move to the design (Class 6).        failures.append("describes a solution: " + ", ".join(design))    # Check 4: every requirement needs a verification method.    if not verify:        # Without one, nobody can say how the requirement will be tested.        failures.append("no verification method")    # Check 5: a non-functional requirement usually needs a number with a unit.    if category == "NFR" and not any(ch.isdigit() for ch in text):        # Only a warning: some quality requirements use a named check instead.        warnings.append("no number: confirm the verification names an objective check")    # Return both lists to the caller.    return failures, warnings  # run() checks a whole set, prints one verdict per requirement, counts the passes.def run(title, requirements):    # Print a heading for this set.    print(f"--- {title} ---")    # passed counts the requirements without any failure.    passed = 0    # Unpack every requirement into its four fields.    for req_id, category, text, verify in requirements:        # Run the five checks on this requirement.        failures, warnings = check(category, text, verify)        # No failure means the requirement can be tested as written.        verdict = "verifiable" if not failures else "NEEDS REWRITE"        # Count the verifiable requirements.        passed += 0 if failures else 1        # Join the problems into one readable note; a dash when there are none.        note = "; ".join(failures) if failures else "-"        # Print the identifier, the category, the verdict and the failures.        print(f"{req_id:<6} {category:<3} {verdict:<13} | {note}")        # Print each warning on its own line, for a person to judge.        for warning in warnings:            # A warning does not change the verdict; it asks for human judgement.            print(f"       warning: {warning}")    # Print the summary line for the set.    print(f"{passed} of {len(requirements)} verifiable")    # Return the number of passes, so the caller can compare the two runs.    return passed  # DRAFTS: Team Falcon's six drafts - ID, the team's category, the text, the check.DRAFTS = [    # D1: two qualities in one sentence, vague words, no number, no check.    ("D1", "NFR", "The app should be fast and easy.", ""),    # D2: a behaviour with no named actor, no limit and no 'shall'.    ("D2", "FR", "Users can cancel.", ""),    # D3: a quality stated with one vague word and no check.    ("D3", "NFR", "Orders shall be secure.", ""),    # D4: a design decision written as if it were a requirement.    ("D4", "FR", "The system shall use a red Cancel button in the top-right corner.", "look at the screen"),    # D5: a limit on the solution - a constraint - already well written.    ("D5", "C", "The product shall run in a web browser without installation.", "open it in 3 browsers"),    # D6: a behaviour with an actor, data and an order - already well written.    ("D6", "FR", "The system shall show the kitchen staff each paid order with its pick-up number and slot, oldest first.", "create 3 orders out of order, check the list"),# The closing bracket ends the list of drafts.]# Check the drafts and keep the number that passed.before = run("Drafts", DRAFTS) # REWRITTEN: the team's new set; D1 became two requirements and D4 left for design.REWRITTEN = [    # From D1: performance, with a number, a unit and a condition.    ("NFR-01", "NFR", "The system shall load the menu page in under 2 seconds on the campus Wi-Fi for a menu of up to 40 items.", "stopwatch, 10 loads, all under 2 s"),    # From D1: usability, measured on first-time users.    ("NFR-03", "NFR", "The system shall let a first-time user complete an order in under 3 minutes without help.", "3 classmates, timed, no hints"),    # From D2: an actor, one behaviour and its time limit.    ("FR-05", "FR", "The system shall let a student cancel their own order until 10 minutes before the chosen pick-up slot.", "try at slot -11 min and at -9 min"),    # From D3: privacy, stated as who may see what.    ("NFR-02", "NFR", "The system shall show a student's allergy note only to that student and to the kitchen screen, never in the manager's summary.", "log in as manager, open the summary, search for the note"),    # D5 kept as constraint C-01.    ("C-01", "C", "The product shall run in a web browser without installation.", "open it in 3 browsers"),    # D6 kept as FR-07.    ("FR-07", "FR", "The system shall show the kitchen staff each paid order with its pick-up number and slot, oldest first.", "create 3 orders out of order, check the list"),# The closing bracket ends the rewritten set.]# Check the rewritten set and keep the number that passed.after = run("Rewritten", REWRITTEN)# Compare the two runs in one line.print(f"Verifiable before: {before} of {len(DRAFTS)}; after: {after} of {len(REWRITTEN)}")

What happens, step by step
  1. VAGUE and DESIGN are tuples of words. A tuple is used because the lists never change while the program runs; the checks only read them.
  2. The function check() receives one requirement and builds two lists: failures (the defects that make it unverifiable) and warnings (points that only a person can judge). It splits the text into lower-case words, without commas and full stops, so that “Easy.” and “easy” compare equal.
  3. Checks 1 to 4 each add a failure: no shall; a vague word (the list comprehension [w for w in VAGUE if w in words] collects all of them); a design word; an empty verification. Check 5 adds only a warning when a non-functional requirement contains no digit — some quality requirements use a named check instead of a number.
  4. The function run() loops over a set of requirements, calls check() for each, prints the verdict and the failures, prints every warning on its own line, and counts the verifiable ones. Watch the grid of the visualisation fill one cell per check.
  5. DRAFTS holds the six drafts as tuples (identifier, kind, text, verification). run("Drafts", DRAFTS) prints six verdicts: D1–D4 need a rewrite, D5 and D6 pass — 2 of 6.
  6. REWRITTEN holds the new set: D1 became NFR-01 and NFR-03, D2 became FR-05, D3 became NFR-02, D4 left for the design, D5 and D6 became C-01 and FR-07. The second run gives 6 of 6, with one warning on NFR-02 for a person to judge.
  7. The last line compares the two runs. Pause on the warning of NFR-02: the program cannot decide whether “never in the manager's summary” is an objective check — a reviewer can, and decides that it is.

Flash-cards
Five flash-cards for Lesson 3
Read the front, say the definition aloud, then click the card to check yourself.
functional requirementclick to flip
States a behaviour or service the system must provide — what it does, for whom, with which input and result. “The system shall let a student cancel their own order until 10 minutes before the slot.”
non-functional requirementclick to flip
States how well the system must perform, or a property of the whole system — performance, security, usability, reliability, maintainability… To be verifiable, it needs a number, a unit and a condition, or a named check.
constraintclick to flip
A limit on the solution or the project set from outside the team — platform, technology, law, budget, deadline, standard. “The product shall run in a web browser without installation.”
verifiable requirementclick to flip
A requirement for which a finite, affordable check exists — test, inspection, analysis or demonstration. Volere calls the measurement its fit criterion.
SRS (Software Requirements Specification)click to flip
The document that states the requirements completely, consistently and verifiably. Reference: ISO/IEC/IEEE 29148 (International Organization for Standardization / International Electrotechnical Commission / Institute of Electrical and Electronics Engineers standard 29148), which superseded IEEE Std 830 (Institute of Electrical and Electronics Engineers Standard 830)-1998 in 2011; current edition 2018. Block 5 is an SRS-Lite (a short Software Requirements Specification).

Active break · 🎯 Fun-quiz · 0:36–0:40 · 4 minutes · slide 31
Functional, non-functional or constraint? Three statements
  1. Read each statement on the screen and vote with your fingers: one finger for a functional requirement, two for a non-functional requirement, three for a constraint.
  2. Statement 1: “The system shall let a student book a study room.”
  3. Statement 2: “Pages shall load in under 2 seconds on the campus Wi-Fi.”
  4. Statement 3: “The system must be written in Python because it is the department standard.”
What to look for — the answer
1 — functional requirement: an action of the system. 2 — non-functional requirement (performance): how well the system acts, with a number. 3 — constraint: a limit on the technology, set outside the team.
Lesson4
Modeling what we learned (1/2): use cases, use-case diagrams and activity diagrams with swimlanes
⏱ 0:40–0:48 · 8 minutes of speech📽 slides 32–40Part D
Goal of the lesson. Define actor, use case, scenario, main flow and alternative flow; write a fully-dressed use case with the Block 5 template; read a use-case diagram with «include» and «extend»; read an activity diagram with swimlanes; turn every scenario of a use case into a test case.
Identifiers used in this lesson: FR-nn = functional requirement number nn; NFR-nn = non-functional requirement number nn; UC-nn = use case number nn; S1–S5 = the five scenarios of the ClubLend use case.
The analysis model: from words to models slides 32–33
Elicitation gave you sentences, and specification turned them into requirements. Elaboration, the third task of Lesson 1, turns them into models that a designer can start from.




analysis model — The set of models that describe what the system must do, in terms of the problem domain: who uses it, for which goals, through which steps, and which things it must remember. It is also called the requirements model; it connects the stakeholders' words to the design.




Pressman and Maxim, chapter 8↗scan, group its elements into three kinds. Scenario-based elements show what the actors do with the system: user stories, use cases, activity diagrams. Class-based elements show the things of the domain: classes, attributes, associations, CRC (Class–Responsibility–Collaborator) cards. Behavioural elements show how the system reacts to events over time: states and transitions. Today you build the first two kinds — scenarios in this lesson, classes in the next.


One rule governs both: the analysis model uses the words of the users, and every technical choice — screens, databases, frameworks — waits for the design of next Tuesday.
Actors, use cases and scenarios slide 34
Ivar Jacobson introduced use cases while he worked on telephone-switching systems at Ericsson; he presented them at the OOPSLA (Object-Oriented Programming, Systems, Languages and Applications conference) conference in 1987 (Object-oriented development in an industrial environment↗scan). Five definitions carry the whole technique.




actor — A role played by a person, an organisation or an external system that interacts with the system and stays outside it. An actor is a role, not a person: Lina can be a member on Monday and a club officer on Tuesday — one person, two actors. The primary actor has the goal; a supporting actor provides a service, such as an e-mail service.


use case — A description of the interactions by which the system helps a primary actor reach one goal of value. It is named as a goal, with a verb and an object, from the actor's point of view: Borrow item, not Loan screen.


scenario — One concrete sequence of steps through a use case, under specific conditions. A use case is the set of all its scenarios.


main flow — The numbered steps of the scenario in which everything succeeds; it is also called the main success scenario.


alternative flow — A variation that branches from a numbered step of the main flow when a condition holds — an error, a refusal, a different choice — and then ends the use case or rejoins the main flow. It is numbered by its step and a letter: 4a is the first alternative at step 4.




The user story of Class 4 opens the conversation about a need; the use case records what the conversation found — the steps, the alternatives, the conditions.
A fully-dressed use case (1/2): the template slide 35
Alistair Cockburn↗scan, in Writing Effective Use Cases (2001), describes three levels of formality: brief (one paragraph), casual (a few paragraphs) and fully dressed (every field, numbered steps). Block 5 asks for three fully-dressed use cases, with the fields of this table.


On the slide:






Field
What it holds






Identifier and name
UC-nn and a goal: verb + object




Primary actor · supporting actors
who has the goal · who helps




Goal
one sentence, in the actor's words




Trigger
the event that starts the use case




Preconditions
what must already be true before it starts




Main flow
numbered steps, alternating actor does / system does




Alternative flows
at least two, each starting at a numbered step: “4a. The item is on loan: …”




Postconditions
what is true after success, and what stays unchanged after a refusal




Related requirements
the identifiers of the FRs (functional requirements) and NFRs (non-functional requirements) that the use case realises






Two habits make the flows good. Write each step as one sentence with a subject and a verb — the member chooses, the system checks — so that it is always clear who does what. Then read every step as a tester would and ask: what if this fails? Each answer that the product must handle becomes an alternative flow.
A fully-dressed use case (2/2): ClubLend, UC-03 Borrow item slide 36
Here is the template filled in by Team Owl for ClubLend, the lending app of a student club that lends board games and books. UC-03 means use case number 3.


On the slide:


UC-03 — Borrow item. Primary actor: member. Supporting actors: club officer; the campus e-mail service, through UC-06. Goal: borrow an available item for 14 days. Trigger: the member selects Borrow on an item of the catalogue. Preconditions: the member is signed in; the item is registered in the catalogue.


Main flow:
1. The member chooses an item and selects Borrow.
2. The system checks that the member has no overdue loan.
3. The system checks that the member holds fewer than 3 active loans.
4. The system checks that the item is available, and reserves it.
5. The system creates the loan, shows a pick-up code valid for 48 hours and sends it by e-mail (include UC-06 Notify member).
6. The club officer checks the code and hands the item over; the system records the hand-over.
7. The system marks the loan active, due back 14 days later.


Alternative flows:
- 2a. The member has an overdue loan: the system refuses and shows the overdue item. The use case ends.
- 3a. The member already holds 3 active loans: the system refuses and shows the limit. The use case ends.
- 4a. The item is on loan: the system offers the waiting list (extension point item on loan, used by UC-05 Join waiting list). The use case ends.
- 6a. The member does not come within 48 hours: the system cancels the loan, releases the item and informs the member. The use case ends.


Postconditions: after success, an active loan links the member and the item, with a due date, and the item is shown as on loan; after a refusal, no loan exists and the item is unchanged. Related requirements: FR-02 (no new loan while one is overdue), FR-03 (loans last 14 days), FR-04 (at most 3 active loans), FR-05 (pick-up within 48 hours), NFR-02 (a member's loan history is visible only to that member and to the club's officers).
The use-case diagram: include and extend slide 37
The use-case diagram of the UML (Unified Modeling Language), published by the OMG (Object Management Group) in version 2.5.1 of the specification, December 2017↗scan, is the overview of the model: a rectangle for the system boundary, with the system's name; the actors outside it; the use cases as ellipses inside it; and a line — an association — between each actor and each use case it takes part in. ClubLend has three actors (member, club officer, campus e-mail service) and six use cases: UC-01 Register item, UC-02 Search catalogue, UC-03 Borrow item, UC-04 Return item, UC-05 Join waiting list and UC-06 Notify member.


Two relationships between use cases are drawn as dashed arrows with a keyword.




«include» — The base use case always performs the behaviour of the included use case, at a given step. The arrow goes from the base to the included use case. Borrow item and Join waiting list both include Notify member: the notification is written once and reused.


«extend» — The extending use case adds optional behaviour to the base use case at an extension point, only when a condition holds. The arrow goes from the extending use case to the base. Join waiting list extends Borrow item at the extension point item on loan — alternative flow 4a.




Use both relationships sparingly. The goals, and the lines from each goal to its actors, are what a reader needs first; a diagram covered with crossing arrows hides them.
Activity diagrams with swimlanes slide 38
A use case is text; the activity diagram of the UML (Unified Modeling Language) draws the same flow, so that every branch is visible at once. Its elements: an initial node (a filled circle) where the flow starts; actions (rounded rectangles); decision nodes (diamonds) whose outgoing arrows carry guards in square brackets, such as [overdue loan]; merge nodes where branches join again; a fork and a join (thick bars) for actions that run in parallel; and final nodes (a circle inside a ring) where the flow ends.




swimlane — A lane of an activity diagram, also called an activity partition, that groups the actions performed by one actor or one system, so that the diagram shows who does each step.




UC-03 needs three lanes: member, ClubLend system, club officer. The flow starts in the member's lane, crosses into the system's lane for the three checks, and moves into the officer's lane for the hand-over. Each diamond is one alternative flow of the text — 2a, 3a, 4a, 6a — and each path from the initial node to a final node is one scenario. When the text and the drawing disagree, one of them is wrong: drawing the diagram checks the text.
From flows to test cases slide 39
This is why the alternative flows matter: every scenario of a use case becomes at least one black-box test case — a test designed from the specification alone, without looking at the code. UC-03 has one main flow and four alternative flows, so it gives at least five test cases.
