S1 to S5 are the five scenarios of the ClubLend example. Lab 07 and Block 7, on November 3, start from exactly this kind of table, and Class 7 adds the cases at the boundaries — 2 active loans or 3, exactly 48 hours or 49. A use case with only a main flow gives one test; the alternatives are where the tests are.

Real-life example
ClubLend: one use-case model, one swimlane diagram, five scenarios
Team Owl · ClubLend · fictional
TaskTeam Owl (fictional) builds ClubLend, the lending app of a student club that lends board games and books: catalogue, loans, returns, waiting list. The team names its actors, draws the use-case diagram (three actors, six use cases, one «include», one «extend»), fully dresses UC-03 Borrow item with four alternative flows, draws its activity diagram in three swimlanes, and lists the five scenarios as the test cases of Block 7.
Relation to the lectureIt applies Lesson 4: actors as roles, use cases as goals, the fully-dressed template of Block 5, «include» and «extend», swimlanes, and the rule that every scenario is one path and at least one test case.
Actors. Member (primary: borrows, returns, joins the waiting list), club officer (primary for registering items; supporting in borrowing and returning: hands items over and takes them back) and the campus e-mail service (a supporting external system). One student, Lina, is both a member and an officer: one person, two actors.


The diagram. Six use cases inside the boundary ClubLend: UC-01 Register item (officer), UC-02 Search catalogue (member), UC-03 Borrow item (member, officer), UC-04 Return item (member, officer), UC-05 Join waiting list (member) and UC-06 Notify member (e-mail service). UC-03 and UC-05 «include» UC-06. UC-05 «extend»s UC-03 at the extension point item on loan.


The text. UC-03 is fully dressed in the lesson: seven steps, four alternative flows (2a overdue loan, 3a limit reached, 4a item on loan, 6a not picked up within 48 hours), postconditions for success and refusal, and five related requirements.


The swimlanes. Member | ClubLend system | club officer. While drawing them, the team could not decide in which lane to put the action release the item of 6a: the first draft of the text did not say whether the officer or the system releases it. The team chose the system — the officer may not be on campus when the 48 hours end — and corrected 6a. The second view found a gap in the first; that is what the activity diagram is for.


The scenarios. Five fictional members, each prepared to follow one scenario: Mira (main flow), Noah (2a), Lea (3a), Omar (4a), Ivy (6a). Each line of the table in the lesson is a test case with its data, its expected path and its expected result.


What the team did not write. No screens, no buttons, no database tables: those belong to the design of Class 6. The privacy harm of the product — who borrowed what is personal data — is written as NFR-02 and listed under Related requirements, so the use case and the specification point to each other.

Demo program
ClubLend — walking UC-03 Borrow item through its five scenarios
demo4_clublend_borrow_usecase.py
TaskExecute the fully-dressed use case UC-03 for five fictional members, each prepared to follow one scenario: test the condition of each numbered step, branch into 2a, 3a, 4a or 6a when it fails, print the path taken, and collect the five scenarios as the black-box test cases of Block 7.
Relation to the lectureLesson 4: a use case is the set of its scenarios — one main flow plus alternative flows numbered by the step where they branch; each scenario is one path through the activity diagram and at least one test case.
The program runs here step by step from a recording of its real execution (nothing runs in your browser). To run it yourself, use any Python 3.8 or newer on your own computer: python3 demo4_clublend_borrow_usecase.py (Legal Notice, section 10↗: your own equipment, your own responsibility; Annex C↗: check every download). Every line of code has a comment line above it.
demo4_clublend_borrow_usecase.pyready
# =============================================================================# CS 330 - Software Engineering · Class 5 · Lesson 4 · Demo 4# ClubLend: walking the use case "Borrow item" through all of its scenarios.## TASK: execute the fully-dressed use case UC-03 "Borrow item" of the fictional#   product ClubLend (Team Owl) for five members, each prepared to follow one#   scenario: walk the numbered steps of the main flow, test the condition of#   each step, branch into the alternative flow (2a, 3a, 4a or 6a) when a#   condition fails, print the path taken, and collect the five scenarios as#   the black-box test cases that Block 7 will need.# RELATION TO THE LECTURE: Lesson 4 - a use case is the set of its scenarios:#   one main flow plus alternative flows that branch from numbered steps; each#   scenario is one path through the activity diagram and one test case.## Educational material - Cyber.SoHo Educational Hub, (c) 2026. Fictional# members and items only. Use is governed by the Cyber.SoHo Legal Notice:# https://cyber-soho.github.io/prevmon/00.01.%20cyber.soho%20-%20legal.html# Run it with any Python 3.8 or newer, on your own computer:#   python3 demo4_clublend_borrow_usecase.py# ============================================================================= # Business rule from FR-04: a member may hold at most 3 active loans at once.MAX_ACTIVE_LOANS = 3# Business rule from FR-03: a loan lasts 14 days.LOAN_DAYS = 14# Business rule from FR-05: an item not picked up within 48 hours is released.PICKUP_HOURS = 48 # REQUESTS: five fictional members, each prepared to follow exactly one scenario.REQUESTS = [    # Mira: no overdue loan, 1 active loan, item free, picks it up after 5 hours.    {"member": "Mira", "overdue": 0, "active": 1, "item_on_loan": False, "pickup_after_h": 5},    # Noah: has 1 overdue loan, so step 2 fails and alternative flow 2a runs.    {"member": "Noah", "overdue": 1, "active": 1, "item_on_loan": False, "pickup_after_h": 5},    # Lea: already holds 3 active loans, so step 3 fails and 3a runs.    {"member": "Lea", "overdue": 0, "active": 3, "item_on_loan": False, "pickup_after_h": 5},    # Omar: the item is already on loan, so step 4 fails and 4a runs.    {"member": "Omar", "overdue": 0, "active": 0, "item_on_loan": True, "pickup_after_h": 5},    # Ivy: everything is fine, but she comes after 60 hours, so 6a runs.    {"member": "Ivy", "overdue": 0, "active": 2, "item_on_loan": False, "pickup_after_h": 60},# The closing bracket ends the list of requests.]  # borrow() walks UC-03 for one request; it returns the path and the outcome.def borrow(request):    # Step 1 always happens: the member chooses an item and selects Borrow.    path = ["1"]    # Step 2: the system checks that the member has no overdue loan.    if request["overdue"] > 0:        # 2a: refuse, show the overdue item; the use case ends here.        path.append("2a")        # Return the path so far and the outcome of 2a.        return path, "refused - an overdue loan must be returned first"    # The condition of step 2 holds: record the step and continue.    path.append("2")    # Step 3: the system checks the limit of active loans.    if request["active"] >= MAX_ACTIVE_LOANS:        # 3a: refuse and show the limit; the use case ends here.        path.append("3a")        # Return the path so far and the outcome of 3a.        return path, f"refused - limit of {MAX_ACTIVE_LOANS} active loans reached"    # The condition of step 3 holds: record the step and continue.    path.append("3")    # Step 4: the system checks that the item is available.    if request["item_on_loan"]:        # 4a: offer the waiting list (the 'Join waiting list' use case extends here).        path.append("4a")        # Return the path so far and the outcome of 4a.        return path, "item on loan - waiting list offered"    # Steps 4 and 5 succeed: the system creates the loan and shows a pick-up code.    path.extend(["4", "5"])    # Step 6: the club officer hands the item over, if the member comes in time.    if request["pickup_after_h"] > PICKUP_HOURS:        # 6a: the code expired, so the system cancels the loan and frees the item.        path.append("6a")        # Return the path so far and the outcome of 6a.        return path, f"loan cancelled - not picked up within {PICKUP_HOURS} hours"    # Steps 6 and 7 succeed: hand-over recorded, loan active.    path.extend(["6", "7"])    # Return the complete main flow and the success outcome.    return path, f"loan active - due back in {LOAN_DAYS} days"  # tests collects one test case per scenario: input member, expected path, outcome.tests = []# Walk the use case once per request, numbering the scenarios S1 to S5.for number, request in enumerate(REQUESTS, start=1):    # Run the use case for this member.    path, outcome = borrow(request)    # Name the scenario: 'main flow' if every step passed, else the alternative.    name = "main flow" if path[-1] == "7" else "alternative " + path[-1]    # Print the scenario number, the member, the path and the outcome.    print(f"S{number} {request['member']:<5} {name:<15} path {' > '.join(path):<22} | {outcome}")    # Keep the scenario as a test case for Block 7.    tests.append((f"S{number}", request["member"], " > ".join(path), outcome)) # Every scenario becomes at least one black-box test case in Block 7.print(f"{len(tests)} scenarios -> {len(tests)} black-box test cases for Block 7")

Program output
Execution steps — every step so far; click a row to go back to it
#linewhereeventwhat changedprinted
What happens, step by step
  1. The three constants hold the business rules of three requirements: MAX_ACTIVE_LOANS (FR-04), LOAN_DAYS (FR-03) and PICKUP_HOURS (FR-05). Names in capital letters mark constants by Python convention; because each rule is written once, a change request touches one line.
  2. REQUESTS is a list of five dictionaries. Each fictional member is designed to follow exactly one scenario: this is test data chosen from the alternative flows, not random data.
  3. The function borrow() follows the numbered steps. path starts with "1"; each if tests the condition of one step. When a condition fails, the function appends the label of the alternative flow (2a, 3a or 4a) and returns at once — the alternative ends the use case, exactly as the text of UC-03 says.
  4. When a condition holds, the step number is appended and the walk continues; path.extend(["4", "5"]) appends two steps in one call. In the visualisation, a marker moves through the swimlanes: member → ClubLend → club officer.
  5. Step 6 compares pickup_after_h with PICKUP_HOURS. Ivy comes after 60 hours, so 6a cancels the loan. A function may contain several return statements; each one returns a tuple (path, outcome), which the caller unpacks into two names.
  6. The main loop numbers the scenarios with enumerate(REQUESTS, start=1), calls borrow(), names the scenario — main flow if the last step is 7, otherwise alternative plus the last label — and prints one line, with the path joined by " > ".
  7. Each scenario is appended to tests as a tuple; the last line prints “5 scenarios -> 5 black-box test cases for Block 7”. Pause there: the path and the outcome are exactly what a tester writes in the expected result column.

Flash-cards
Five flash-cards for Lesson 4
Read the front, say the definition aloud, then click the card to check yourself.
actorclick to flip
A role played by a person, an organisation or an external system that interacts with the system and stays outside it. One person can play several roles; the primary actor has the goal, a supporting actor provides a service.
use caseclick to flip
A description of the interactions by which the system helps a primary actor reach one goal of value; named verb + object (“Borrow item”). Introduced by Ivar Jacobson, presented in 1987.
main flow and alternative flowclick to flip
Main flow: the numbered steps of the scenario in which everything succeeds. Alternative flow: a variation that branches at a numbered step when a condition holds — “4a. The item is on loan: …” — then ends or rejoins.
«include» and «extend»click to flip
«include»: the base use case always performs the included one (arrow from the base to the included use case). «extend»: optional behaviour added at an extension point when a condition holds (arrow from the extending use case to the base).
swimlaneclick to flip
A lane of a UML (Unified Modeling Language) activity diagram (an activity partition) that groups the actions of one actor or system, so the diagram shows who does each step. Each path from start to end is one scenario — and at least one test case.

Lesson5
Modeling what we learned (2/2): the domain model, CRC (Class–Responsibility–Collaborator) cards, validation, traceability — and function points
⏱ 0:48–0:56 · 8 minutes of speech📽 slides 41–50Part D
Goal of the lesson. Build a domain model with analysis classes, attributes, associations and multiplicities; find classes with nouns and CRC (Class–Responsibility–Collaborator) cards; validate requirements with a checklist; check traceability in both directions; count function points with the course's simplified method and compare the result with the Block 3 estimate.
Identifiers used in this lesson: US-nn = user story number nn (for example US-03, user story 3); FR-nn = functional requirement number nn; NFR-nn = non-functional requirement number nn; UC-nn = use case number nn.
The domain model slides 41–42
Use cases describe what the actors do. The second half of the analysis model describes the things they talk about.




domain model — A model of the important concepts of the problem domain — the things that the users talk about and that the product must remember — with their attributes and the associations between them. It is drawn as a UML (Unified Modeling Language) class diagram without operations, and it contains no software parts: no screens, no database tables, no controllers.


analysis class — A class of the domain model: a concept of the problem, such as Report or Category, of which the product keeps many objects.


attribute — A named property whose value every object of the class holds: a report has a trackingNumber, a description, a submittedAt time and a currentStatus.


association — A structural relationship between two classes, labelled with a verb phrase that reads in one direction: a report is filed under a category.


multiplicity — The number of objects of one class that can be linked to one object of the class at the other end of an association, written as an interval: 1 (exactly one), 0..1 (at most one), 0..* (any number) or 1..* (at least one).




Read multiplicities one end at a time, starting from one object. A report is filed under exactly 1 category; a category groups 0..* reports. Team Heron's product, SafeCampus, gives one more example worth noticing: a report is submitted by 0..1 reporter. The zero is a requirement: SafeCampus accepts anonymous reports, and the domain model shows it before anyone writes a line of code.
Finding the classes: nouns and CRC (Class–Responsibility–Collaborator) cards slide 43
Where do the classes come from? From the text you already have. Underline the nouns in your user stories and use cases — your textbook calls this a grammatical parse (Pressman and Maxim, chapter 8↗scan) — and treat each noun as a candidate. Then filter the list with four questions. Must the product remember information about this thing? If not, drop it. Is it a single value, such as a status or a date? Then it is an attribute, not a class. Is it a screen, a button, a database or the system itself? Then it belongs to the design. Do two nouns mean the same thing — incident and report? Then keep one, and write the other in the glossary.


The verbs give the associations: a moderator changes a status, a report is located at a place.




CRC (Class–Responsibility–Collaborator) card — An index card with three parts: the class name at the top; its responsibilities on the left — what it knows and what it does; its collaborators on the right — the other classes it needs to fulfil those responsibilities.




Kent Beck and Ward Cunningham proposed the cards at OOPSLA (Object-Oriented Programming, Systems, Languages and Applications conference) in 1989 (A Laboratory for Teaching Object-Oriented Thinking↗scan). The team uses them in a role-play: someone reads a scenario aloud, and whoever holds the card of the class responsible for each step speaks. A responsibility that nobody holds reveals a missing class; a card that never speaks is probably not needed. Five to eight cards survive in Block 5.
Validating the requirements and the models slide 44
Before a team builds on its models, it validates them — the sixth task of Lesson 1. The usual technique is a review: the authors walk two or three readers through the specification and the models, and the readers look for defects with a checklist. Your partner team, and the written feedback on block5-draft, play that role in this course. The checklist below gathers the questions of the textbook and the characteristics of ISO/IEC/IEEE 29148 (International Organization for Standardization / International Electrotechnical Commission / Institute of Electrical and Electronics Engineers standard 29148) in seven lines.


On the slide:


    

  1. Source — does every requirement name the story or the interview answer it comes from?
    2. 

  2. Verifiable — does every requirement have a verification line that a tester could run?
    3. 

  3. Unambiguous — does every requirement have one reading only; are words with two meanings in the glossary?
    4. 

  4. Consistent — do two requirements contradict each other, or a requirement and a constraint?
    5. 

  5. Feasible — can it be built within the constraints of time, money and platform?
    6. 

  6. Modelled — is every functional requirement realised by a use case, and is every class of the domain model used by at least one use case?
    7. 

  7. In scope — is every requirement inside the Block 3 scoping decision?
    8. 



Questions 1, 6 and 7 can be answered mechanically, from a table. That table is the traceability matrix.
Traceability slide 45


traceability — The ability to follow each requirement backward to its source and forward to the models, the code and the tests that realise it.


traceability matrix — A table with one row per requirement and one column per related artefact — user story, use case, test, function-point element — in which an empty cell shows a gap.




Backward traceability answers: why does this requirement exist? Forward traceability answers: where is it realised, and how will we know it works? Each kind of gap has its own correction:


    

  • a requirement without a story or interview answer has no known source: find one, or delete the requirement — it is an extra that no stakeholder asked for;
    • 

  • a requirement without a use case is not modelled yet: write the use case;
    • 

  • a story without a requirement is a missing requirement: write one, or park the story outside the scope;
    • 

  • a requirement without a test is not verified yet: that column fills in Block 7.
    • 



Lesson 1 gave one more reason. When a change request arrives, the matrix shows at once the stories, use cases and tests linked to each requirement it changes; the impact analysis starts from those links, exactly as in the HabitHub example. Block 5 delivers the matrix as a table in the file or as the spreadsheet 05-traceability_TEMPLATE.csv, with its three checks: every functional requirement has a story and a use case; every story appears at least once; every use case appears at least once.
Function points (1/2): the five elements slide 46
Block 3 estimated the size of your product in lines of code, before a single requirement existed. Now that the requirements exist, you can measure the size of what they ask for.




function point — A unit of functional size: it measures how much functionality the software provides to its users, counted from the requirements and independent of the programming language.




Allan Albrecht created the method at IBM (International Business Machines) and published it in 1979. Today the IFPUG (International Function Point Users Group) maintains it, and its counting rules are an international standard, ISO/IEC 20926 (International Organization for Standardization / International Electrotechnical Commission standard 20926), described on its official page↗scan. The count looks at five kinds of elements, seen from the user's side of the system boundary:


    

  • EI (External Input) — data or a command that enters the system from outside and changes stored data: submit a hazard report.
    • 

  • EO (External Output) — information that leaves the system and contains calculated or generated data: a monthly summary per category; a confirmation with a newly generated tracking number.
    • 

  • EQ (External Inquiry) — stored data retrieved and shown without calculation and without changing anything: check the status of a report.
    • 

  • ILF (Internal Logical File) — a group of logically related data that the system itself maintains: the reports, the categories.
    • 

  • EIF (External Interface File) — a group of logically related data that the system only reads, maintained by another system: the campus directory, the building list.
    • 



The first three are transactions, the last two are data groups. A data group is a group that a user would recognise, not a database table: the status history of a report belongs to the report group.
Function points (2/2): the count, the factor and its use slides 47–48
The full method rates each element as low, average or high. The course uses the average weights only:


UFP (Unadjusted Function Points) = 4 × EIs (External Inputs) + 5 × EOs (External Outputs) + 4 × EQs (External Inquiries) + 10 × ILFs (Internal Logical Files) + 7 × EIFs (External Interface Files)


The traditional method then adjusts the count with 14 general system characteristics — data communication, performance, online data entry, complexity of processing, ease of installation and nine others — each rated from 0 (no influence) to 5 (essential). Their sum ΣF gives the VAF (Value Adjustment Factor):


FP (Function Points) = UFP (Unadjusted Function Points) × (0.65 + 0.01 × ΣF)


ΣF lies between 0 and 70, so the factor lies between 0.65 and 1.35; an average product, ΣF = 35, gives exactly 1.00. ISO/IEC 20926 (International Organization for Standardization / International Electrotechnical Commission standard 20926) standardises only the unadjusted count; the adjustment is an older, optional step that the textbook still teaches. Block 5 uses ΣF = 35.


A worked example for the board: 6 EIs (External Inputs), 4 EOs (External Outputs), 3 EQs (External Inquiries), 2 ILFs (Internal Logical Files) and 1 EIF (External Interface File). UFP (Unadjusted Function Points) = 24 + 20 + 12 + 20 + 7 = 83; with ΣF = 35, FP (Function Points) = 83 × 1.00 = 83.


What is the count for? It converts into a size: a common rule of thumb is about 50 lines of code per function point for a typical web language. Team Heron counts 69 function points for SafeCampus — 3,450 lines, 3.45 KLOC (thousands of lines of code) — against the 3 KLOC (thousands of lines of code) of its Class 3 size list: the two estimates agree within about 15 %, and both lie far above the roughly 580 lines that the team's hours buy according to the formula of Class 3. Two independent estimates that agree are worth more than one, and neither replaces the real pace that Block 7 will measure. The method has two weak points to remember for the Final: counting needs training and judgement, and the number of lines per function point varies widely between languages and teams.

Real-life example
SafeCampus: classes from nouns, a matrix with three gaps, and 69 function points
Team Heron · SafeCampus · fictional
TaskTeam Heron (fictional) builds SafeCampus: a student or a staff member reports a hazard on campus — a broken stair light, a wet floor, a blocked exit — under their name or anonymously, and follows its status until it is fixed. The team finds its analysis classes from the nouns of its stories, checks them with a round of index cards, draws the domain model, checks its traceability matrix in both directions, corrects three gaps, and counts the function points of what remains, to compare with its Class 3 estimate.
Relation to the lectureIt applies Lesson 5: nouns and CRC (Class–Responsibility–Collaborator) cards, analysis classes with attributes and multiplicities, validation with the traceability matrix in both directions, and the Numbers corner — function points with the average weights.
The stories (fictional): US-01 report a hazard with its category and location, named or anonymous · US-02 follow my report · US-03 as a moderator, see the open reports and change their status · US-04 as the campus security office, a monthly summary per category and location · US-05 as the campus security office, add a hazard category · US-06 attach a photo to a report.


Nouns → classes. The candidates were student, staff member, hazard, report, incident, category, location, building, moderator, status, photo, map, app, screen, notification. Kept: Report, Category, Location, StatusChange, Moderator, Reporter. Rejected: student and staff member (two roles of one class, Reporter); hazard and incident (synonyms of report — the glossary says “a report describes one hazard”); status (an attribute of Report; a change of status, with its time and its moderator, is a class); app and screen (the system and the design); photo (US-06, parked); map (no story asks for it); notification (an output of the system, not a thing it must remember).


The index-card round. Reading UC-03 Moderate report aloud: the Moderator card says “I change the status”; the Report card says “I record a StatusChange and update my current status”; the StatusChange card says “I know the new status, the time, the note and the moderator.” Nobody needed a Database card, which confirms that the model contains no design.


The domain model. Reporter 0..1 — 0..* Report (submits) · Report 0..* — 1 Category (is filed under) · Report 0..* — 1 Location (is located at) · Report 1 — 0..* StatusChange (has) · StatusChange 0..* — 1 Moderator (is made by). The 0..1 at the Reporter end matches NFR-02: when a report is anonymous, the stored report contains no field that identifies the reporter — verified by inspecting the stored record of an anonymous test report.


The traceability check (the demo of this lesson): FR-08 add a hazard category has a story but no use case → the team writes UC-05; FR-09 a campus map of all reports has neither a story nor a use case → nobody asked for it, deleted; US-06 attach a photo has no requirement → outside the Block 3 scope, parked. Eight requirements and five stories remain, with no empty cell. FR-08 matters: in Class 4, the security office had not yet decided which categories it wants, so categories are data that it can add, not code that the team must change.


The count. EI (External Input) 3 (submit a report · change a status · add a category) = 12 · EO (External Output) 3 (confirmation with a tracking number · status-change notice to a named reporter · monthly summary) = 15 · EQ (External Inquiry) 2 (check the status of my report · moderators' list of open reports) = 8 · ILF (Internal Logical File) 2 (reports · categories) = 20 · EIF (External Interface File) 2 (campus directory · building list) = 14 → UFP (Unadjusted Function Points) = 69, FP (Function Points) = 69. The comparison sentence of Block 5: 69 function points × 50 = 3,450 lines, close to the 3,000 lines of our Class 3 list; the two estimates agree, so we keep the scoping decision of Block 3 and measure our real lines per function point in Block 7.

demo5_safecampus_trace_fp.py
TaskCheck the traceability matrix of SafeCampus — every requirement needs a user story (its source) and a use case (its model); every story needs at least one requirement — list the gaps, apply the team's three decisions, then count the function points with the course's average weights and convert them into lines of code to compare with Block 3.
Relation to the lectureLesson 5: backward traceability (requirement → story), forward traceability (requirement → use case), the gaps and the decisions they force; function points with the average weights; the comparison with the Block 3 estimate.
The program runs here step by step from a recording of its real execution (nothing runs in your browser). To run it yourself, use any Python 3.8 or newer on your own computer: python3 demo5_safecampus_trace_fp.py (Legal Notice, section 10↗: your own equipment, your own responsibility; Annex C↗: check every download). # =============================================================================# CS 330 - Software Engineering · Class 5 · Lesson 5 · Demo 5# SafeCampus: a traceability check in both directions, then a function-point# count of the requirements that survive it.## TASK: check the traceability matrix of the fictional product SafeCampus#   (Team Heron) - every requirement needs a user story (its source) and a use#   case (its model); every story needs at least one requirement - list the#   gaps, apply the team's three decisions, then count the function points#   with the course's simplified average weights and convert them into an#   estimate of lines of code to compare with the Block 3 estimate.# RELATION TO THE LECTURE: Lesson 5 - traceability (backward to the source,#   forward to the model and the tests) and the Numbers corner: function points.## Educational material - Cyber.SoHo Educational Hub, (c) 2026. Fictional data# only. Use is governed by the Cyber.SoHo Legal Notice, Terms of Use and Acceptable Use Policy:# https://cyber-soho.github.io/prevmon/00.01.%20cyber.soho%20-%20legal.html# Run it with any Python 3.8 or newer, on your own computer:#   python3 demo5_safecampus_trace_fp.py# ============================================================================= # The six user stories of SafeCampus, US-01 to US-06.STORIES = ["US-01", "US-02", "US-03", "US-04", "US-05", "US-06"] # Each requirement maps to (its user story, its use case, its function-point element).requirements = {    # Submit a hazard report, named or anonymous: from US-01, modelled in UC-01, an external input (EI).    "FR-01": ("US-01", "UC-01", "EI"),    # Confirmation with a tracking number: an external output (EO), derived data.    "FR-02": ("US-01", "UC-01", "EO"),    # Check the status of a report by its tracking number: an external inquiry (EQ), stored data shown.    "FR-03": ("US-02", "UC-02", "EQ"),    # A moderator changes the status of a report: an external input (EI).    "FR-04": ("US-03", "UC-03", "EI"),    # Notify a named reporter of each status change: an external output (EO).    "FR-05": ("US-02", "UC-02", "EO"),    # Moderators list the open reports by category and date: an external inquiry (EQ).    "FR-06": ("US-03", "UC-03", "EQ"),    # Monthly summary per category and building: an external output (EO).    "FR-07": ("US-04", "UC-04", "EO"),    # Add a hazard category: from US-05, but no use case models it yet.    "FR-08": ("US-05", None, "EI"),    # A campus map of all reports: no story asked for it, no use case models it.    "FR-09": (None, None, "EQ"),# The closing brace ends the dictionary of requirements.} # gaps collects every problem the check finds, as readable sentences.gaps = []# Backward and forward check, one requirement at a time.for req_id, (story, use_case, element) in requirements.items():    # Backward traceability: a requirement without a story has no known source.    if story is None:        # Record the gap and what to do about it.        gaps.append(f"{req_id}: no user story -> find its source or delete it")    # Forward traceability: a requirement without a use case is not modelled.    if use_case is None:        # Record the gap and what to do about it.        gaps.append(f"{req_id}: no use case -> model it")# Collect the stories that at least one requirement points back to.traced = {story for story, _, _ in requirements.values() if story is not None}# A story that no requirement points back to is a missing requirement.for story in STORIES:    # Test the story against the traced set.    if story not in traced:        # Record the gap and what to do about it.        gaps.append(f"{story}: no requirement -> write one, or park the story")# Print every gap the check found.for gap in gaps:    # One gap per line.    print("GAP  " + gap) # Decision 1: nobody asked for the campus map, so FR-09 is deleted.del requirements["FR-09"]# Decision 2: the team writes use case UC-05 'Add hazard category' for FR-08.requirements["FR-08"] = ("US-05", "UC-05", "EI")# Decision 3: US-06 (attach a photo) is outside the Block 3 scope, so it is parked.STORIES.remove("US-06")# Print the decisions and the size of the cleaned matrix.print(f"FIX  FR-09 deleted, UC-05 written for FR-08, US-06 parked -> {len(requirements)} requirements, {len(STORIES)} stories") # The data groups: two kept by SafeCampus (ILF), two read from other systems (EIF) -# the campus directory for signing in, the building list of the facilities service.DATA_GROUPS = {"ILF": ["Report", "Category"], "EIF": ["Campus directory", "Building list"]}# The course's simplified average weights for the five elements.WEIGHTS = {"EI": 4, "EO": 5, "EQ": 4, "ILF": 10, "EIF": 7} # counts starts every element at zero.counts = {"EI": 0, "EO": 0, "EQ": 0, "ILF": 0, "EIF": 0}# Every remaining requirement adds one transaction of its element type.for req_id, (story, use_case, element) in requirements.items():    # Add one to the counter of this element.    counts[element] += 1# The two kinds of data group are counted from DATA_GROUPS.counts["ILF"] = len(DATA_GROUPS["ILF"])# External interface files: data read by SafeCampus but kept by other systems.counts["EIF"] = len(DATA_GROUPS["EIF"]) # ufp accumulates the unadjusted function points, element by element.ufp = 0# Multiply each count by its weight and add the product to the total.for element, weight in WEIGHTS.items():    # Points contributed by this element.    points = counts[element] * weight    # Add them to the running total.    ufp += points    # Print the line of the counting table.    print(f"{element:<3} {counts[element]} x {weight:>2} = {points:>2}") # The sum of the 14 influence factors; 35 means 'average' and gives a factor of 1.00.sum_of_factors = 35# The value adjustment factor: 0.65 + 0.01 x the sum of the factors.vaf = 0.65 + 0.01 * sum_of_factors# The adjusted function points.fp = ufp * vaf# Print the two totals.print(f"UFP = {ufp}; FP = {ufp} x {vaf:.2f} = {fp:.0f}") # Rule of thumb from Lab 05: about 50 lines of code per function point for a web language.lines = fp * 50# Print the size in KLOC (thousands of lines of code), to compare with Block 3.print(f"Size estimate: {fp:.0f} FP x 50 lines = {lines:,.0f} lines = {lines / 1000:.2f} KLOC")
Visualisation of the lecture idea
Variables (yellow = changed by this step)
Program output
Execution steps — every step so far; click a row to go back to it
#linewhereeventwhat changedprinted
What happens, step by step
  1. STORIES lists the six user stories. The dictionary requirements maps each requirement to a tuple (story, use case, function-point element). None marks an empty cell of the matrix — exactly what a reviewer looks for.
  2. The first loop unpacks each tuple in the for line itself: for req_id, (story, use_case, element) in requirements.items(). A requirement without a story fails the backward check; one without a use case fails the forward check. FR-08 and FR-09 light up in the matrix of the visualisation.
  3. A set comprehension builds traced, the set of stories that at least one requirement points back to; the underscore _ names the values that this line does not need. The loop over STORIES then finds US-06, a story without a requirement.
  4. The three decisions: del removes FR-09; assigning a new tuple to FR-08 adds UC-05; STORIES.remove("US-06") parks the story. Eight requirements and five stories remain, and the matrix has no empty cell.
  5. WEIGHTS holds the five average weights. The counting loop adds one transaction per requirement to counts; two lines then set the data groups from DATA_GROUPS, because data groups come from the domain, not from single requirements. Watch the bars grow.
  6. The second loop multiplies each count by its weight and accumulates ufp: 12 + 15 + 8 + 20 + 14 = 69. With the sum of the 14 factors at 35, vaf = 0.65 + 0.35 = 1.00, so fp = 69.
  7. The last line converts 69 function points × 50 lines into 3,450 lines, printed as 3.45 thousand lines — the number Team Heron compares with the 3,000 lines of its Class 3 list. The format {lines:,.0f} prints the thousands separator.

Flash-cards
Five flash-cards for Lesson 5
Read the front, say the definition aloud, then click the card to check yourself.
domain modelclick to flip
A model of the concepts of the problem domain — the things the users talk about and the product must remember — with attributes and associations; a UML (Unified Modeling Language) class diagram without operations and without software parts (screens, tables, controllers).
multiplicityclick to flip
How many objects of one class can be linked to one object at the other end: 1, 0..1, 0..* or 1..*. “A report is filed under exactly 1 category; a category groups 0..* reports.”
CRC (Class–Responsibility–Collaborator) cardclick to flip
An index card with the class name, its responsibilities (what it knows and does) and its collaborators (the classes it needs). Kent Beck and Ward Cunningham, 1989; used in a role-play of the scenarios.
traceabilityclick to flip
Following each requirement backward to its source (story, interview) and forward to its use case, design, code and tests. In the traceability matrix, every gap is an empty cell.
function pointclick to flip
A unit of functional size counted from five elements — external inputs, external outputs, external inquiries, internal logical files, external interface files. Average weights 4, 5, 4, 10, 7; FP (Function Points) = UFP (Unadjusted Function Points) × (0.65 + 0.01 × ΣF). Allan Albrecht, IBM (International Business Machines): first published in 1979, refined in 1983–84.
Self-test
Formative quiz — Lesson 5: 4 multiple-choice + 2 multiple-select questions
⚑ This quiz is FORMATIVE, not summative: it is here to help you learn, nothing is recorded or sent anywhere, and it does NOT count towards your final grade. The graded assessments of CS 330 are the project Blocks with engagement (30 %), the Mid-Term (30 %, Tuesday, November 17) and the Final (40 %, Tuesday, January 19).
A multiple-choice question has one right answer among four options. A multiple-select question has six options; the number of right answers is shown in round brackets. Your own work, in your own words ([Legal Notice, section 18](https://cyber-soho.github.io/prevmon/00.01.%20cyber.soho%20-%20legal.html#18-academic-integrity-and-submitted-work)).
Multiple-choice question Q5.1 · Which of these belongs in a domain model?
Hint: Would a user of SafeCampus use the word?
Multiple-choice question Q5.2 · “A report is submitted by 0..1 reporter.” What does the multiplicity 0..1 at the reporter end mean?
Hint: Start from one report and count the reporters linked to it.
Multiple-choice question Q5.3 · A product has 5 external inputs, 3 external outputs, 4 external inquiries, 3 internal logical files and 2 external interface files. What is its unadjusted function-point count, with the average weights 4, 5, 4, 10, 7?
Hint: Multiply each count by its weight, then add the five products.
Multiple-choice question Q5.4 · In the SafeCampus check, FR-09 “a campus map of all reports” has no user story and no use case. What did the team do, and why?
Hint: Backward traceability asks: why does this requirement exist?
Multiple-select question Q5.5 · Which of these are transaction elements of a function-point count? (3 right answers)
Hint: Three of the five elements move data across the boundary; two are groups of data.
Multiple-select question Q5.6 · Which statements about traceability are true? (4 right answers)
Hint: Backward to the source, forward to models and tests.
Active break · 🧘 Zen-break, then 🃏 flash-cards · 0:56–1:00 · 4 minutes · slide 50
One quiet minute, then a flash-card sprint on the modeling terms
  1. One minute of quiet: stand up, roll your shoulders, look at something far away, and breathe in for four counts and out for six. Nothing to do — on purpose.
  2. Three minutes in pairs: partner A reads a term from the slide; partner B defines it in one sentence, without notes. After six terms, swap. The terms: elicitation · functional requirement · non-functional requirement · constraint · Software Requirements Specification · use case · actor · alternative flow · domain model · multiplicity · Class–Responsibility–Collaborator card · traceability · function point.
  3. Put a mark next to every term that you could not define: those cards come first in tonight's review.
What to look for — the answer
Every definition is on the flash-cards of the five lessons, in the module and in the Study Hub.
After the hour — Studio and Home Sprint
Studio (100′, with your team) — Lab 05, summary slide 51
Lab 05 and its templates are published separately; this is only the plan of the Studio.
TimeStepWhat happens
1:10–1:20Step 1 · Set upCopy the template to /docs/05-srs.md; copy the scoping decision of Block 3; name two or three harms of the product; list six to eight user stories.
1:20–1:40Step 2 · Elicitation roundTeams paired with a different product; six questions (two open, two closed, two probing); interview each other for six minutes each way; three answers and one surprise.
1:40–2:10Step 3 · SRS-Lite (a short Software Requirements Specification)8–12 FRs (functional requirements), exactly 5 NFRs (non-functional requirements) — one each for performance, security or privacy, usability, reliability and maintainability — and 3 constraints — each with an ID (identifier), a source and a verification line.
2:10–2:30Step 4 · Use-case modelActors; a use-case diagram with at least five use cases; two fully-dressed use cases with at least two alternative flows each.
2:30–2:45Step 5 · Domain modelCRC (Class–Responsibility–Collaborator) round with index cards; 5–8 analysis classes with attributes, associations and multiplicities.
2:45–2:50Step 6 · First function-point countTick each element of the FR (functional requirement) list as EI (External Input), EO (External Output), EQ (External Inquiry), ILF (Internal Logical File) or EIF (External Interface File); UFP (Unadjusted Function Points) and FP (Function Points) with ΣF = 35.
2:50–3:00Wrap-upThe Block 5 box and the deadline; exit ticket: “One requirement you rewrote to make it testable — before and after.”
Exit ticket, one sentence on paper: “One requirement you rewrote to make it testable — before and after.”
Home Sprint (120′) slide 52
  • Finish Block 5 — Lab 05, Steps 7 to 11, one hour at most: the third fully-dressed use case, the domain model checked against the FRs (functional requirements), the traceability matrix, a careful second function-point count and one comparison sentence with Block 3, then commit, tag and post.
  • Recommended: tag a first version block5-draft by Sunday, October 25, 23:59 — written feedback arrives before the Mid-Term. The final version, tag block5, is due Sunday, December 20, 2026, 23:59, like every Block.
  • Read Pressman and Maxim, 9th edition, chapter 7 (Understanding Requirements) and chapter 8 (Requirements Modeling), and the function-point pages of chapter 25.
  • Optional, never graded — Numbers practice: two function-point exercises in /docs/numbers.md (announced here; they are provided separately).
  • Flash-cards: add this week's thirteen terms to your deck and review last week's twelve.
Where this goes next — summary only. Lab 07 / Block 7 (Tuesday, November 3) is created separately, in its own class. In one sentence: it will take today's verification lines, use-case scenarios and the empty test column of the traceability matrix, and turn them into a first test plan, the first code with at least six unit tests, black-box test tables and a complexity analysis.
